d.t: A task.
d.e: I've got a job for you: could you wash the dishes?

d.t: An economic role for which a person is paid.
d.e: That surgeon has a great job.

d.t: (in noun compounds) Plastic surgery.
d.e: He had a nose job.

d.t: (in noun compounds) A sex act.
d.e: hand job

d.t: (computing) A task, or series of tasks, carried out in batch mode (especially on a mainframe computer).
A public transaction done for private profit; something performed ostensibly as a part of official duty, but really for private gain; a corrupt official business.
(informal) A robbery or heist.
d.e: a bank job

d.t: Any affair or event which affects one, whether fortunately or unfortunately.
(colloquial) A thing or whatsit (often used in a vague way to refer to something whose name one cannot recall).
d.e: Pass me that little job with the screw thread on it.

d.t: (UK, slang, law enforcement, uncountable) The police as a profession, act of policing, or an individual police officer.
(vulgar, slang) Synonym of penis.
(obsolete) A sudden thrust or stab; a jab or punch.
(intransitive) To do odd jobs or occasional work for hire.
(intransitive) To work as a jobber.
(intransitive, professional wrestling slang) To take the loss, usually in a demeaning or submissive manner.
(transitive, trading) To buy and sell for profit, as securities; to speculate in.
(transitive, often with out) To subcontract a project or delivery in small portions to a number of contractors.
d.e: We wanted to sell a turnkey plant, but they jobbed out the contract to small firms.

d.t: (intransitive) To seek private gain under pretence of public service; to turn public matters to private advantage.
To hire or let in periods of service.
d.e: to job a carriage

d.t: (intransitive, now rare, regional) To peck (of a bird); (more generally) to poke or prod (at, into).
(transitive) To pierce or poke (someone or something), typically with a sharp or pointed object; to stab.
(transitive, now Australia) To hit (someone) with a quick, sharp punch; to jab.
(transitive) To connect or combine into one; to put together.
d.e: The plumber joined the two ends of the broken pipe.

d.t: (intransitive) To come together; to meet.
d.e: Parallel lines never join.

d.t: (intransitive) To enter into association or alliance, to unite in a common purpose.
(transitive) To start working on or participating in a project.
d.e: He joined season 2 of the television show.

d.t: (transitive) To come into the company of.
d.e: I will join you in watching the football game as soon as I have finished my work.

d.t: (transitive) To become a member of.
d.e: Many children join a sports club.

d.t: (computing, databases, transitive) To produce an intersection of data in two or more database tables.
d.e: By joining the Customer table on the Product table, we can show each customer's name alongside the products they have ordered.

d.t: To unite in marriage.
(obsolete, rare) To enjoin upon; to command.
To accept, or engage in, as a contest.
d.e: to join encounter, battle, or issue

d.t: An act of joining or the state of being joined; a junction or joining.
An intersection of piping or wiring; an interconnect.
(computing, databases) An intersection of data in two or more database tables.
(computing) The act of joining something, such as a network.
(algebra) The lowest upper bound, an operation between pairs of elements in a lattice, denoted by the symbol ∨.
(algebraic geometry) The smallest linear space containing both of two given linear spaces.
Factually right, correct; factual.
d.e: It is a just assessment of the facts.

d.t: Rationally right, correct.
Morally right; upright, righteous, equitable; fair.
d.e: It looks like a just solution at first glance.

d.t: Proper, adequate.
Only, simply, merely.
d.e: Just plant a few tomatoes, unless you can freeze or dry them.

d.t: (sentence adverb) Used to reduce the force of an imperative; simply.
d.e: Just follow the directions on the box.

d.t: (sentence adverb) Used to increase the force of an imperative; simply, without questioning.
d.e: I'm tired of playing games – just get it done.

d.t: Used to convey a less serious or formal tone.
d.e: I just called to say "hi".

d.t: (degree) Absolutely, positively.
d.e: It is just splendid!

d.t: Barely, hardly, scarcely.
Exactly, precisely, perfectly.
d.e: He wants everything just right for the big day.

d.t: (slang) Expressing dismay or discontent.
A joust, tournament.
To joust, fight a tournament.
